section.title: Boundaries and orientation
section.p: A form changes sign when orientation reverses. So before we state the theorem, we must make the signs automatic. The boundary of an interval, a region, a surface, or a solid should inherit its orientation from the object it bounds.

subsection.title: Oriented intervals and endpoints
subsection.p: Start with the old one-dimensional picture.

The interval I=[a,b] is oriented from left to right. Its boundary consists of two endpoints, but the endpoints do not have the same sign: \boxed{\partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}.} The right endpoint is positive. The left endpoint is negative.
This is exactly the sign pattern in the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a). In forms language, f is a 0-form and \int_{\partial[a,b]} f=f(b)-f(a).

statement.p:
Let I=[2,5] with the usual left-to-right orientation, and let f(x)=x^2+1. Then \partial I=\{5\}-\{2\}. So
\int_{\partial I} f \amp = f(5)-f(2) \amp = 26-5 \amp = 21.
If the same interval is given the opposite orientation, then its boundary becomes \{2\}-\{5\}, and the integral becomes -21.

subsection.p: A point by itself has no direction to walk. Its orientation is only a sign: +P \qquad\text{or}\qquad -P. That is enough for 0-forms.

The sign convention can be remembered by the word outward. At the right endpoint, the outward direction points in the positive direction of the interval. At the left endpoint, the outward direction points in the negative direction. So the right endpoint gets +, and the left endpoint gets -.

subsection.title: Oriented plane regions and boundary curves
subsection.p: A region in the xy-plane has the standard orientation dx\wedge dy. This means that the ordered pair of directions \text{positive }x\text{-direction first, positive }y\text{-direction second} is positive.
The boundary of such a region is oriented so that the region stays on your left as you walk along the boundary.
For a region without holes, this means counterclockwise.

figure.caption: A positively oriented plane boundary keeps the region on the left.

example.title: A rectangle and its positive boundary

statement.p: Let R=[0,4]\times[0,3], oriented by dx\wedge dy. Then \partial R is the rectangle walked counterclockwise: (0,0)\to(4,0)\to(4,3)\to(0,3)\to(0,0).

If \omega=x\,dy, then the bottom and top edges contribute 0, because dy=0 there. The right edge has x=4,\qquad 0\le y\le3, so \int_{\text{right edge}}x\,dy=\int_0^3 4\,dy=12. The left edge has x=0, so it contributes 0. Therefore \boxed{\int_{\partial R} x\,dy=12.} If we walk the rectangle clockwise, the answer becomes -12.

subsection.p: For a region with a hole, the same region on the left rule gives two different-looking directions.
The outer boundary is counterclockwise. The inner boundary is clockwise.

figure.caption: The inner boundary of a positively oriented annulus is walked clockwise.

subsection.p: This is not a special exception. It is the same rule. If you walk around the hole clockwise, the material of the annulus stays on your left.

exercise.title: Why does the hole turn the other way?

statement.p: The outer edge of the annulus is walked counterclockwise, but the inner edge around the hole is walked clockwise. Without computing anything, explain why these two opposite-looking directions are really the same rule. What single phrase ties them together?

hint.p: Stand on the boundary and ask: on which side does the gray material sit as you walk? Trace the inner circle clockwise in your mind and watch where the region lies.

definition.title: Positive boundary orientation in the plane

statement.p: Let R be a plane region oriented by dx\wedge dy. The positive orientation of \partial R is the one for which the region stays on the left as the boundary is traveled.
For a region without holes, this is counterclockwise. For an inner boundary around a hole, this is clockwise.

subsection.title: Oriented surfaces and boundary curves
subsection.p: A surface in space is oriented by choosing one of its two sides. Equivalently, we choose a continuous unit normal vector field \mathbf n on the surface.

For a parametrized surface \mathbf r(u,v), the normal direction attached to the parameter order (u,v) is \mathbf r_u\times \mathbf r_v. Swapping the parameters reverses the orientation: \mathbf r_v\times \mathbf r_u = -\mathbf r_u\times \mathbf r_v.
Once the surface orientation is chosen, the boundary curve orientation is forced.

statement.p: We say that picking a side of the surface (a normal \mathbf n) forces the direction you walk the boundary. What would go wrong if you tried to flip the boundary direction while keeping the same normal \mathbf n? Why can't the two choices be made independently?

hint.p: Point your right thumb along \mathbf n and let your fingers curl. There is only one way they curl. Think about what Stokes' theorem \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega would say if the two sides disagreed by a sign.

example.title: A disk with two possible orientations

statement.p: Let D be the unit disk in the xy-plane: x^2+y^2\le1.
If D is oriented by the upward normal \mathbf n=\mathbf k, then its boundary circle is oriented counterclockwise when viewed from above: \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi.
If D is oriented by the downward normal \mathbf n=-\mathbf k, then the same boundary circle is oriented clockwise when viewed from above: \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,-\sin t,0), \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi.

subsection.p: The rule is the right-hand rule.
Point your right thumb in the chosen normal direction. Your fingers curl in the positive boundary direction.

figure.caption: Changing the surface normal reverses the boundary orientation. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

image.shortdescription: A 3D disk with an upward normal and counterclockwise boundary arrow.
A 3D disk with an downward normal and clockwise boundary arrow.

subsection.p: There is also a version of the region on the left rule for surfaces.
Imagine standing on the surface with your head pointing in the chosen normal direction. Walk along the boundary in the positive direction. The surface should stay on your left.

definition.title: Boundary orientation of an oriented surface

statement.p: Let S be an oriented surface with chosen normal direction \mathbf n. The positive orientation of \partial S is the direction given by the right-hand rule: the thumb points in the direction of \mathbf n, and the fingers curl in the positive boundary direction.
Equivalently, when walking along the boundary with head in the normal direction, the surface stays on the left.

subsection.p: This is the orientation used in Stokes' theorem: \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega. The sign of the boundary integral depends on the side of the surface we chose.

subsection.title: Oriented solids and boundary surfaces
subsection.p: A solid region in ordinary space has the standard orientation dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. The boundary of a solid is a surface, and its positive orientation is the outward one.
This is the orientation used for flux. A flux integral over the boundary of a solid uses the outward normal.

example.title: The boundary orientation of a box

statement.p:
Let E=[0,2]\times[0,3]\times[0,4]. The boundary \partial E has six faces. Each face is oriented by its outward normal.
\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Face} \amp \text{Outward normal} \amp \text{Positive area form on the face} \\ \hline x=2 \amp \mathbf i \amp dy\wedge dz\\[1mm] x=0 \amp -\mathbf i \amp dz\wedge dy\\[1mm] y=3 \amp \mathbf j \amp dz\wedge dx\\[1mm] y=0 \amp -\mathbf j \amp dx\wedge dz\\[1mm] z=4 \amp \mathbf k \amp dx\wedge dy\\[1mm] z=0 \amp -\mathbf k \amp dy\wedge dx \end{array}

For instance, the top face z=4 has outward normal \mathbf k, so its positive surface orientation is dx\wedge dy. The bottom face z=0 has outward normal -\mathbf k, so its positive surface orientation is dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy.

subsection.p: This sign pattern is not arbitrary. It comes from the same outward first rule that worked for intervals and plane regions.

subsection.title: The outward-first convention
subsection.p: All boundary orientations in this book come from one convention.

figure.caption: Outward first in four settings. At a boundary point, place the outward direction \nu_{\mathrm{out}} before the indicated boundary direction or directions; the resulting ordered list agrees with the orientation of the interval, region, surface, or solid. (Interactive: drag either scene to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

image.shortdescription: In a 3D view, an oriented interval has outward directions at its endpoints, and a planar disk has an outward direction followed by the positive boundary tangent.
A rotatable oriented surface disk and solid box show the outward-first directions at a boundary point and on the top face.

exercise.title: What is the boundary of a boundary?

statement.p: The boundary \partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\} is a pair of signed points, and a point has no boundary at all, so \partial\partial[a,b] is empty. Looking at the outward-first picture, why should it be no accident that taking the boundary twice always leaves nothing behind? What does that say about the edges where two faces of the box meet?

hint.p: Each shared edge of the box belongs to two faces, and those two faces walk it in opposite directions. You don't need a formula here, just imagine the contributions of neighboring faces meeting along an edge.

statement.p: Let M be an oriented k-dimensional object, where k=1,2, or 3. At a smooth boundary point, let \nu_{\text{out}} be the outward direction normal to the boundary but tangent to M.

subsection.p: This convention may look abstract, so let us test it in the three familiar cases.
The theorem needs exactly these signs. If one sign is reversed, the two sides of Stokes' theorem disagree by a minus sign.
The boundary has now become a signed object. That is the missing piece. A form lives on the boundary, its derivative lives inside, and the orientations are ready to make the two integrals comparable.
The next step is to state the theorem that has been hiding behind the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, and the divergence theorem.
